result:
I'm done: `final.py` scores **88.1** on the search split, using **6 of the 24** scorer calls. The baseline scores about 1.0. I couldn't score it on the held-out split, because `./score` only covers the search split. So the only out-of-sample checks are my own: a local harness using random inputs I never tuned on (held-out seeds, where it ran 104x faster than the reference) and a second input shape with long records (about 12x faster). It matched the reference pair for pair on every input I tried, including hundreds of small edge-case inputs.

| | search score |
|---|---|
| baseline | ~1.0 |
| first working version (c1) | 72.3 |
| tuned version (c9) | 80.5 / 80.4 |
| **final (c15)** | **87.6 / 88.1** |

Time: about 9 minutes (05:51–06:00) of the default ~15-minute budget I followed from the skill. I stopped early because the last few tries all landed within measurement noise.

**Why it's faster:**
- **Identical records are grouped first.** Each record becomes its word set, built with C-level `map`/`dict(zip)` calls. Records with identical word sets are paired directly, with no comparison.
- **Words are put in one fixed order, rarest first.** Each word set is sorted that way. For two sets to be at least 80% alike, they must share at least one of the first few words of each sorted set, roughly the first fifth. So each set is only compared against sets that share one of those words, and only if its size is within the possible range (at least 4/5 of the larger set's size). Survivors get the exact check `9·|A∩B| ≥ 4·(|A|+|B|)`, which is the same test as the spec's `5·|A∩B| ≥ 4·|A∪B|`.
- **Sets of 1–3 words are left out of the comparison step.** Two different sets of that size can never reach 80% with anything. This step took the score from 80 to 88, so the real data must contain many short records.
- The file imports nothing, so there is no import-time cost.

**Approaches tried:**
- **Plain alphabetical word order** instead of rarest-first: 5x, far worse. The frequency order is what makes it fast.
- **Long-record filter (PPJoin-style position check):** 26% faster on long records but 4% slower on short ones. Officially it scored 76.5 against 80.5, so I dropped it.
- **Finding small pairs by deleting one word at a time:** if the larger set has 8 words or fewer, a match is only possible when the smaller set is a subset with exactly one word fewer. Looking those up by hashing was 7% slower than the main method.
- **Counting word frequencies on a sample**, or with the stdlib C helper `_collections._count_elements`: about equal to the plain count. Not worth an unusual private import.
- **Small loop tweaks** (skipping one-off words, a `min()` path for small sets, skipping probes for 4-word sets): all within noise.

**Candidate log** (scorer calls used: 6 of 24):

| candidate | harness | scorer | kept? |
|---|---|---|---|
| c1 prefix filter + grouping | 88x | 72.3 | replaced |
| c2 cheaper word ranking | 95.6x | – | kept |
| c3 alphabetical order | 5.2x | – | dropped |
| c4 micro-optimisations | ≈ c2 | – | kept |
| c5 `_count_elements` | −2% time | – | dropped |
| c6/c9 `min()` path + specialised short prefixes | −2% time | 80.5, 80.4 | kept |
| c7 sampled frequencies | ≈ | – | dropped |
| c8 C-level grouping | −1% time | – | kept |
| c10/c11 position filter | +7% short, −27% long | 76.5 | dropped |
| c12a/b, c13 | ≈ or worse | – | dropped |
| c15 skip sets of ≤3 words | −5% time | 87.6, 88.1 | **final** |
| c16 one-word-deletion hashing | +7% time | – | dropped |
| c17 no probes for 4-word sets | ≈ | – | dropped |

The other `c*.py` candidates, `harness.py`, `bench.py` and `bench2.py` are still in the folder next to `final.py`.
